Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a common fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis. It infects leaves and fruit, causing olive-green to black velvety spots that turn corky and scab-like.
symptoms: Olive-green to dull dark brown velvety spots on leaf surfaces
Yellowing and premature leaf drop
Corky, brown, cracked scabs on fruit skin
Deformed, stunted fruit growth
causes: Fungal pathogen Venturia inaequalis
Prolonged leaf wetness during spring rains (6-9+ hours)
Overwintering fungal spores on fallen leaf litter from previous seasons
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (such as Captan, Mancozeb, or Myclobutanil) starting at green tip stage
Use bio-fungicide sprays containing Bacillus subtilis for organic management
Prune affected twigs and heavily infected foliage to reduce fungal spore density
Consult local agricultural extension specialists before applying synthetic chemical fungicides
prevention: Rake, destroy, or compost fallen autumn leaves thoroughly to eliminate overwintering spores
Prune tree canopies annually to allow maximum sunlight penetration and rapid air drying
Plant scab-resistant apple cultivars (such as Liberty, Enterprise, or Prima)
Avoid overhead irrigation that wets foliage for prolonged periods

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot is caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. It attacks leaves (producing 'frog-eye' leaf spots), limbs (cankers), and fruit (rotting into firm, mummified black spheres).
symptoms: Purple-bordered circular leaf spots with light brown centers ('frog-eye' spots)
Dark sunken cankers with cracked margins on bark and branches
Firm brown rot on fruit starting near the blossom end, expanding in concentric rings
Shriveled, black mummified apples remaining attached to twigs
causes: Fungal pathogen Botryosphaeria obtusa
Spore dissemination by splashing rain and wind
Wounds from pruning, insects, or frost damage serving as entry points
treatment: Prune out dead wood, twigs, and branch cankers 6-8 inches below infected areas
Remove all mummified apples from trees and orchard floors immediately
Apply copper-based fungicides or Captan from silver tip through post-bloom stages
Consult certified agronomists for region-specific spray schedules
prevention: Maintain vigorous tree health through balanced fertilization and proper soil pH
Sanitize pruning tools between cuts with 70% isopropyl alcohol or 10% bleach
Control insect pests to prevent fruit and branch wounding
Ensure proper branch spacing to facilitate rapid drying

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is caused by the heteroecious fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. It requires two hosts (apple trees and Eastern red cedars/junipers) to complete its lifecycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange or reddish circular spots on upper leaf surfaces
Small raised black dots (pycnia) within leaf spots
Fringed tube-like fungal projections (aecia) under leaves in late summer
Distorted fruit with raised yellow spots near the calyx end
causes: Fungal pathogen Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae
Proximity to infected Eastern Red Cedar or Juniper trees within 1-2 miles
Wind-blown spores released from cedar galls during warm spring rains
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (such as Myclobutanil or Mancozeb) starting when cedar galls swell in spring
Spray organic sulfur or neem formulations during early foliage emergence
Consult local extension educators for targeted timing based on regional spore release alerts
prevention: Remove nearby Eastern Red Cedar and juniper trees within 1 mile if feasible
Plant rust-resistant apple cultivars (such as Freedom, Liberty, or Redfree)
Inspect nearby ornamental junipers and prune out brown gall swellings in winter

Apple___healthy.description: The apple foliage shows vibrant green pigmentation, normal leaf expansion, and no signs of fungal, bacterial, or pest damage.
symptoms: Smooth, deep green leaves with crisp margins
No lesions, scabs, rust spots, or chlorosis
Healthy vegetative shoot development
causes: Optimal horticultural care, balanced nutrition, and appropriate orchard management
treatment: No disease treatment required
Maintain regular watering, pruning, and nutritional baseline
prevention: Continue routine monitoring for early pest or disease appearance
Apply dormant oil sprays in early spring to prevent aphid and scale infestations
Ensure balanced annual fertilization based on soil testing

Blueberry___healthy.description: The blueberry plant exhibits clean, vigorous foliage with vibrant green leaves and no evidence of fungal blight, mummy berry, or nutrient deficiencies.
symptoms: Uniform green leaves without spotting, necrosis, or curling
Sturdy stem development and normal budding
Healthy root and cane growth
causes: Appropriate soil acidity (pH 4.5 - 5.5), balanced moisture, and good drainage
treatment: No disease treatment required
Maintain acidic soil conditions with pine bark or elemental sulfur
prevention: Mulch root zones with pine needles or wood chips to maintain moisture and soil acidity
Water regularly at root level using drip irrigation
Prune older canes annually to stimulate vigorous new growth

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on cherry is caused by the fungus Podosphaera clandestina. It produces a white, talcum powder-like fungal coating on young leaves, shoots, and fruit.
symptoms: White powdery fungal patches on undersides and tops of young leaves
Upward curling, distortion, and blistering of expanding leaves
Stunted shoot tip growth ('rosetting')
Deformed, unmarketable fruit with web-like russeting
causes: Fungal pathogen Podosphaera clandestina
High relative humidity combined with warm, dry daytime temperatures (15-27°C)
Dense, unpruned canopies restricting airflow
treatment: Apply potassium bicarbonate or sulfur sprays at the first sign of mildew
Use systemic fungicides (such as DMI or strobilurin fungicides) where disease pressure is severe
Apply horticultural oils or bio-fungicides for organic orchards
Always follow agricultural extension timing guidelines
prevention: Prune trees to open up canopies for optimal air circulation and solar penetration
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization that produces excessive succulent green growth
Monitor orchard weekly from petal fall through harvest

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: Cherry foliage is robust, vibrant green, and free from fungal mildew, bacterial cankers, or shot-hole lesions.
symptoms: Vibrant green leaves with serrated margins and no discoloration
Clean petioles and healthy terminal shoot growth
Firm, unblemished fruit development
causes: Well-drained soil, adequate sunlight, and routine preventative orchard hygiene
treatment: No disease treatment required
Continue balanced orchard nutrition and hydration
prevention: Apply copper bactericide during autumn leaf fall to prevent bacterial cankers
Prune only in dry weather during mid-summer to reduce fungal infection risks
Maintain weed-free tree bases and balanced soil organic matter

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is a destructive foliar disease of maize caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis. It creates rectangular, vein-bounded tan lesions that can cause extensive premature leaf blighting.
symptoms: Small tan spots expanding into long, rectangular lesions bounded by leaf veins
Lesions turning gray with velvety fungal sporulation during humid periods
Severe blighting and premature drying of upper canopy leaves
Stalk lodging due to reduced photosynthetic reserves
causes: Fungal pathogen Cercospora zeae-maydis
Continuous no-till corn production leaving infested residue on soil surface
Prolonged warm (24-30°C), humid weather (>90% RH) and persistent morning dews
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides (such as QoI + DMI combinations or SDHIs) around tasseling (VT to R1) if disease reaches ear leaf
Consult crop advisors to determine economic thresholds before spraying
prevention: Plant hybrid corn varieties with strong genetic resistance to Gray Leaf Spot
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops (such as soybeans or alfalfa) for at least 1-2 years
Incorporate or manage infected crop debris through tillage where conservation practices permit

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust of maize is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. It produces characteristic cinnamon-brown powdery pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
symptoms: Small cinnamon-brown, circular to elongated pustules scattered across leaf surfaces
Pustules rupturing the leaf epidermis to release powdery orange-brown spores
Pustules turning dark brown to black late in the season (teliospores)
Yellowing and necrosis around heavily infected leaf areas
causes: Fungal pathogen Puccinia sorghi
Wind-blown urediniospores carried north on air currents from southern regions
Cool to moderate temperatures (16-24°C) with high humidity and leaf wetness
treatment: Apply registered foliar fungicides if pustules appear on upper leaves before silking on susceptible inbreds/hybrids
Treatment is rarely needed for commercially resistant field corn hybrids
prevention: Plant rust-resistant corn hybrids containing Rp resistance genes
Plant early in the season to allow crops to mature before spore migration peaks
Scout fields regularly starting at early whorl stage

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern Corn Leaf Blight (NCLB) is caused by Exserohilum turcicum. It creates large, cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions that can devastate photosynthesizing leaf area.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped lesions (1 to 6 inches long) on leaves
Lesions initially grayish-green, turning tan with dark sporulation in damp weather
Merging of lesions causing complete blighting and death of foliage
Reduced kernel filling and lower test weights
causes: Fungal pathogen Exserohilum turcicum
Survival in infected corn leaf debris on soil surface
Moderate temperatures (18-27°C) combined with frequent rain or heavy dew
treatment: Apply protective or systemic fungicides (triazoles/strobilurins) between VT and R2 stages if disease is present on ear leaves
Seek agronomist evaluation for field-specific economic injury thresholds
prevention: Select resistant corn hybrids with polygenic and Ht single-gene resistance
Rotate fields away from corn for at least 1-2 seasons
Manage surface crop residue to accelerate natural decomposition

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: The maize plant exhibits robust stalk architecture, broad green leaves with clear venation, and no signs of blights, rusts, or pest feeding.
symptoms: Broad, deep green leaves with crisp margins and no chlorotic streaks
Sturdy stalk structure and strong brace roots
Normal tassel and silk emergence
causes: Optimal soil fertility (balanced N-P-K), adequate moisture, and effective weed management
treatment: No disease treatment required
Maintain side-dress nitrogen schedule and moisture management
prevention: Conduct routine scouting throughout whorl, tasseling, and grain fill stages
Maintain soil drainage to prevent root rot in low-lying areas
Practice balanced crop nutrition based on annual soil tests

Grape___Black_rot.description: Grape black rot is caused by Guignardia bidwellii. It is one of the most destructive grape diseases in warm, humid climates, attacking leaves, shoots, and fruit clusters.
symptoms: Small, circular reddish-brown spots with dark borders on leaves
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) arranged in rings within leaf lesions
Berries turning soft and brown, rapidly shriveling into hard, wrinkled black mummies
Sunken black cankers on young canes and tendrils
causes: Fungal pathogen Guignardia bidwellii
Overwintering mummies on the vine or ground releasing ascospores in spring
Warm temperatures (21-32°C) with persistent leaf and berry wetness
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (such as Mancozeb, Captan, or Myclobutanil) starting at 1-inch shoot growth through 4 weeks post-bloom
Use copper-based sprays or Bordeaux mixture for organic viticulture
Consult viticulture specialists for cultivar-specific fungicide timing
prevention: Physically remove and destroy all mummified fruit clusters during winter pruning
Canopy management: shoot thinning, positioning, and leaf pulling to maximize sunlight and airflow
Keep the ground beneath the vine canopy free from tall weeds

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca is a complex fungal wood disease caused by Phaeoacremonium and Phaeomoniella species. It induces characteristic 'tiger-stripe' leaf patterns and spotted, unmarketable berries.
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' chlorotic and necrotic patterns between leaf veins
Small, dark purple or brown spots on berry skin ('measles')
Cracking, drying, and dropping of infected berries
Internal wood showing dark brown to black vascular streaking or spongy white rot
causes: Complex of wood-rotting fungal pathogens entering through pruning wounds
Stress factors such as drought, high temperatures, and vine age
treatment: No chemical cure exists for infected trunk wood
Prune out symptomatic cordons or trunks down to healthy white wood and retrain new shoots
Paint pruning wounds with wound sealants or biological protectants (Trichoderma)
prevention: Delay winter pruning until late in the dormant season when wound healing is faster
Avoid large pruning wounds during wet weather
Disinfect pruning shears regularly with disinfectant solution

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Grape leaf blight, caused by Pseudocercospora vitis (Isariopsis clavispora), produces irregular dark brown spots on foliage that lead to premature defoliation late in the season.
symptoms: Irregularly shaped dark brown or black spots with well-defined margins on leaves
Spots coalescing into large necrotic blighted areas
Under-leaf surfaces showing a faint olive-brown fungal bloom
Premature foliage drop weakening winter vine cold hardiness
causes: Fungal pathogen Pseudocercospora vitis
High humidity and prolonged late-season rainfall
Poor canopy airflow in overgrown vineyards
treatment: Apply protective copper or Mancozeb sprays if late-season defoliation threatens vine reserves
Prune affected canes and rake fallen foliage after harvest
prevention: Ensure proper trellis management and canopy leaf removal around the fruiting zone
Maintain adequate vine nutrition to sustain healthy foliage late into harvest
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation

Grape___healthy.description: Grapevine foliage is lush, broad, and vibrant green with clean fruit clusters, showing no signs of fungal mildew, black rot, or esca.
symptoms: Broad, intact leaves with vibrant green chlorophyll and smooth venation
Clean shoots, tendrils, and developing fruit clusters
Normal internode spacing and healthy cane maturation
causes: Balanced soil nutrients, optimal canopy microclimate, and appropriate pest management
treatment: No disease treatment required
Continue regular canopy management and vineyard maintenance
prevention: Maintain canopy shoot positioning for maximum airflow and sun exposure
Perform winter dormant pruning during dry conditions
Monitor weekly for early signs of powdery mildew or insect pests

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Huanglongbing (HLB), or Citrus Greening, is a devastating bacterial disease caused by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus and transmitted by the Asian Citrus Psyllid vector.
symptoms: Asymmetric, blotchy yellow mottling across leaf blades
Yellowing of leaf veins ('corky veins') and small, upright chlorotic leaves
Severe twig dieback and canopy thinning
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green at the blossom end ('greening')
Dark, aborted seeds inside sliced citrus fruit
causes: Bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus
Vector transmission by the Asian Citrus Psyllid (Diaphorina citri)
Grafting with infected budwood
treatment: There is currently no cure for HLB-infected citrus trees
Apply intensive nutritional and foliar micronutrient sprays to prolong tree productivity
Rogue out and destroy confirmed infected trees to protect neighboring citrus groves
Control psyllid insect vector populations using systemic and contact insecticides
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free citrus trees from registered nurseries
Install yellow sticky traps to monitor psyllid populations
Release biological control agents (such as Tamarixia radiata parasitoid wasps)
Quarantine and avoid moving citrus plant materials from HLB-positive zones

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot on peach is caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It damages leaves, twigs, and fruit, causing 'shot-hole' foliage loss and deeply cracked fruit lesions.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown and drop out ('shot-hole' effect)
Severe yellowing of leaf tips and premature defoliation
Dark sunken spots with gummy exudate on peach fruit skin
Spring cankers on young twigs causing branch dieback
causes: Bacterial pathogen Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni
Bacterial overwintering in twig cankers and bud scales
Wind-blown rain, driving storms, and sandy abrasive soils
treatment: Apply copper bactericides during dormant season and early bud break
Apply oxytetracycline sprays during bloom and petal fall stages in severe pressure areas
Consult local extension specialists for strict bactericide resistance management
prevention: Plant resistant peach cultivars (such as Harrow Diamond, Redhaven, or Intrepid)
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization that produces tender, susceptible shoot growth
Plant windbreaks around sandy orchards to reduce sand-abrasion entry wounds

Peach___healthy.description: Peach foliage is vigorous, lanceolate, and vibrant green with no shot-holes, bacterial spotting, leaf curl, or twig cankers.
symptoms: Smooth, bright green lance-shaped leaves with healthy margins
Sturdy young shoots with clean bark
Unblemished fruit development
causes: Adequate soil drainage, full sun exposure, and balanced nutrition
treatment: No disease treatment required
Maintain fruit thinning and soil moisture
prevention: Apply a preventive dormant copper spray in autumn or early spring to prevent peach leaf curl
Prune annually in open-center vase format for solar penetration
Monitor for peach tree borer and fungal diseases regularly

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of bell pepper is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria. It causes water-soaked spots on leaves and fruit, causing severe defoliation and sunscald.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked circular to irregular lesions on leaves
Lesions turning dark brown with yellow halos
Severe leaf dropping leading to exposed, sunscalded pepper fruit
Raised, warty, scab-like spots on developing peppers
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria
Contaminated seed or infected transplant seedlings
Warm temperatures (24-30°C) with splashing rain or overhead irrigation
treatment: Apply copper bactericide combined with Mancozeb spray at 7-10 day intervals
Use bio-bactericide sprays (such as Bacillus amyloliquefaciens)
Prune heavily infected lower leaves and dispose of them off-site
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds and disease-free certified transplants
Rotate crops away from solanaceous plants (tomatoes, peppers, potatoes) for 2-3 years
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering to keep foliage dry
Sanitize all garden tools and stakes with 10% bleach solution

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: Bell pepper foliage is rich, dark green, and sturdy with crisp leaf margins and healthy blossoming.
symptoms: Glossy, deep green leaves free from spots or curling
Strong central stem and healthy branching nodes
Healthy white flower blossoms and firm fruit sets
causes: Well-draining warm soil, consistent moisture, and balanced N-P-K nutrients with calcium
treatment: No disease treatment required
Maintain consistent soil moisture to prevent blossom end rot
prevention: Mulch soil around base to preserve moisture and suppress weeds
Ensure calcium availability in soil to prevent physiological disorders
Monitor weekly for aphids, whiteflies, or thrips

Potato___Early_blight.description: Potato early blight is caused by the fungal pathogen Alternaria solani. It primarily attacks older foliage, creating characteristic concentric target-board brown spots.
symptoms: Dark brown to black circular spots with distinct concentric rings ('target board')
Yellowing chlorotic tissue surrounding expanding lesions
Progressive dieback starting on lower, mature leaves and moving upward
Sunken, dark, leathery dry rot lesions on potato tubers
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani
Overwintering fungal mycelium in crop debris and solanaceous weeds
Alternating wet and dry cycles with temperatures between 24-29°C
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (such as Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or Copper Hydroxide)
Use bio-fungicide sprays containing Bacillus subtilis for organic cultivation
Prune and remove severely infected lower leaves
prevention: Rotate crops away from potatoes and tomatoes for at least 3 years
Provide balanced nitrogen and potassium fertilization to prevent premature vine senescence
Irrigate early in the morning so foliage dries rapidly during the day
Destroy all infected plant residue after harvest

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans (the historical cause of the Irish Potato Famine). It spreads with devastating speed in cool, damp weather.
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked dark brown to black lesions on leaves and stems
White, fuzzy fungal/oomycete growth on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Rapid collapse, rotting, and foul odor of entire vine canopies within days
Brown to purplish dry rot penetrating into the flesh of potato tubers
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans
Infected seed tubers or volunteer potatoes acting as primary inoculum
Cool, damp conditions (10-21°C) with relative humidity near 100%
treatment: Apply systemic and contact fungicides (such as Metalaxyl, Dimethomorph, or Chlorothalonil) immediately upon detection
Destroy and bag heavily infected vines immediately to prevent neighborhood spore spread
Always notify local agricultural extension services during active late blight outbreaks
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free seed potatoes
Eliminate all cull piles and volunteer potatoes from previous crops
Plant late blight-resistant potato cultivars (such as Defender or Elba)
Hill soil generously around potato bases to prevent spores from washing down to tubers

Potato___healthy.description: The potato plant displays lush, bright green foliage with strong stems and no indications of blight lesions or viral mottling.
symptoms: Vibrant green compound leaves without necrotic spots or yellowing
Sturdy upright vine canopy and healthy branching
Clean leaf surfaces free from fungal mold or insect damage
causes: Proper hilling, well-drained fertile soil, and optimal moisture management
treatment: No disease treatment required
Continue regular hilling and balanced watering
prevention: Hill plants as vines grow to keep developing tubers completely shaded from sunlight
Scout foliage weekly, especially under damp or cool weather conditions
Apply organic mulch to retain soil moisture and reduce soil splashing

Raspberry___healthy.description: Raspberry canes and foliage are vigorous, vibrant green, and completely free from anthracnose, cane blight, spur blight, or rust.
symptoms: Healthy serrated green leaves with clear venation
Vigorous primocane and floricane growth with clean bark
Firm, unblemished berry development
causes: Well-drained soil, regular cane pruning, and good trellis airflow
treatment: No disease treatment required
Maintain annual cane pruning and drip irrigation
prevention: Prune out spent floricanes down to ground level immediately after harvest
Thin new primocanes to 4-6 canes per foot of row for air circulation
Avoid overhead watering that wets the cane canopy

Soybean___healthy.description: Soybean plant demonstrates healthy trifoliate leaves, strong nodulation, and no signs of Frogeye leaf spot, rust, or root rots.
symptoms: Lush, uniform trifoliate green leaves with no lesions or chlorosis
Active nitrogen-fixing root nodules (pink internal color)
Healthy pod set and filling
causes: Balanced soil fertility, appropriate rhizobium inoculation, and good weed control
treatment: No disease treatment required
Continue monitoring canopy health through pod fill
prevention: Practice crop rotation with non-legume crops (corn, wheat)
Plant certified seed treated with protective fungicide and rhizobium inoculant
Scout for soybean aphids, bean leaf beetles, and foliar blights during R1-R4 stages

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew of cucurbits is caused by Podosphaera xanthii (syn. Sphaerotheca fuliginea). It covers leaves with a powdery white fungal growth, causing premature drying and sunburned fruit.
symptoms: White powdery fungal spots developing on both upper and lower leaf surfaces and petioles
Powder rapidly expanding to cover entire leaf blades
Infected leaves turning yellow, then brown, brittle, and dying prematurely
Reduced fruit yield and sunburned squash due to lost canopy shade
causes: Fungal pathogen Podosphaera xanthii
Airborne conidia spores drifting from nearby cucurbit plantings
High humidity combined with warm, shaded conditions (20-28°C)
treatment: Apply potassium bicarbonate (e.g. Armicarb), sulfur, or neem oil sprays at first sign of white spots
Apply systemic cucurbit fungicides (such as Quintec or Procure) for commercial plantings
Spray a diluted organic milk solution (40% milk, 60% water) in direct sunlight as a natural remedy
prevention: Select powdery mildew-resistant squash varieties (PM-resistant hybrids)
Space plants generously (3-4 feet apart) to promote airflow and sun penetration
Plant in full sunlight and avoid shaded field corners
Clean up all crop residue at the end of the growing season

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Strawberry leaf scorch is caused by the fungus Diplocarpon earlianum. It creates numerous small dark purple spots on leaves that expand, causing foliage to appear burned and scorched.
symptoms: Numerous irregular, small purple or dark brown spots on upper leaf surfaces
Centers of spots remaining dark (unlike common leaf spot which turns white)
Spots coalescing, causing leaf margins to curl upward and turn brown/scorched
In severe cases, death of leaves, flowers, and fruit stems
causes: Fungal pathogen Diplocarpon earlianum
Overwintering in old infected leaves and crowns
Frequent rains and prolonged leaf wetness in spring and summer
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (such as Captan or Copper Hydroxide) at early spring leaf emergence
Remove and discard severely scorched leaves after harvest
Renovate strawberry beds after harvest by mowing foliage above crowns
prevention: Plant certified disease-free strawberry plants
Plant in raised beds or well-drained soil with wide plant spacing
Use straw mulch to prevent soil splashing while keeping fruit elevated
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation

Strawberry___healthy.description: Strawberry foliage is vibrant green, glossy, and compact with clean crowns, strong runners, and abundant blossoms.
symptoms: Healthy trifoliate leaves with vibrant green coloration and clean margins
Strong crown architecture with no rot or discolored petioles
Firm, unblemished fruit and healthy white flower blossoms
causes: Proper raised bed drainage, clean straw mulch, and balanced nutrition
treatment: No disease treatment required
Maintain consistent drip irrigation and runner management
prevention: Renovate June-bearing beds annually after fruiting concludes
Apply straw mulch in late autumn to protect crowns from winter frost heave
Maintain drip irrigation lines under mulch to keep foliage dry

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Tomato bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas species (X. euvesicatoria, X. perforans). It produces dark, greasy leaf spots, defoliation, and scabby fruit lesions.
symptoms: Small (less than 1/8 inch), water-soaked, dark circular spots on leaves
Spots turning dark brown to black with yellow halos
Severe foliage yellowing and defoliation, exposing fruit to sunscald
Small, raised, scab-like blister spots with dark margins on green tomatoes
causes: Bacterial pathogen Xanthomonas species
Contaminated seed or infected transplant seedlings
Warm temperatures (24-30°C) with rain splashing, overhead watering, or driving winds
treatment: Apply fixed copper bactericides combined with Mancozeb to enhance control
Spray biological controls (such as Bacillus subtilis or bacteriophage solutions)
Prune infected lower foliage during dry weather to minimize inoculum
Consult local extension educators for copper-resistant Xanthomonas strain management
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds (hot-water treated) and disease-free transplants
Rotate crops away from tomatoes and peppers for at least 2-3 years
Water exclusively at soil level using drip irrigation
Sanitize stakes, cages, and pruning tools with 10% bleach between plants

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Tomato early blight is a widespread fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It causes target-board concentric spots on lower foliage, progressive defoliation, and stem cankers.
symptoms: Dark brown to black circular lesions with distinct concentric target rings on older leaves
Yellowing chlorosis surrounding leaf spots, leading to premature leaf drop
Sunken dark lesions on stems ('collar rot' on seedlings)
Dark, leathery, sunken spots with concentric rings at the stem end of fruit
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani
Overwintering in soil and crop debris from previous solanaceous plantings
Soil splashing onto lower leaves during rains or overhead watering
treatment: Apply bio-fungicides (Bacillus subtilis, Trichoderma) or organic copper fungicides
Apply protective chemical fungicides (Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, Azoxystrobin) on a 7-14 day schedule
Prune off the bottom 12-18 inches of foliage to stop soil-borne spore splash
Always follow label safety directions and pre-harvest intervals
prevention: Apply a 2-3 inch layer of clean straw or plastic mulch around plant bases
Stake or cage tomato plants to keep foliage elevated off the soil
Water only at the root zone via drip lines; avoid wetting foliage in the evening
Rotate garden beds away from tomatoes, potatoes, and peppers for 3 years

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Tomato late blight is caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans. It is an aggressive, destructive disease that can destroy entire tomato crops in just a few days during wet weather.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked dark green to purplish-brown lesions on leaves and stems
White fuzzy mildew-like growth on the undersides of infected leaves during humid weather
Rapid collapse, browning, and rotting of entire foliage canopy with a strong odor
Firm, greasy, golden-brown to dark sunken rot on green and ripe tomato fruit
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans
Airborne sporangia carried on wind currents from miles away
Cool to moderate temperatures (15-22°C) with persistent fog, heavy dews, or rainfall
treatment: Apply targeted fungicides (such as Mandipropamid, Dimethomorph, or Chlorothalonil) immediately at first confirmation
Remove, bag, and bury heavily infected plants immediately to prevent neighborhood-wide spore spread
Do not compost late blight-infected plants in home compost piles
prevention: Plant late blight-resistant tomato cultivars (such as Mountain Magic, Defiant PhR, or Iron Lady)
Ensure wide plant spacing (3 feet minimum) to promote rapid foliage drying
Eliminate nearby volunteer tomatoes and cull potato piles
Sign up for local agricultural late blight tracking and alert networks

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Tomato leaf mold is caused by the fungus Passalora fulva (syn. Cladosporium fulvum). It is especially prevalent in greenhouses and high tunnels with high relative humidity.
symptoms: Pale green to yellowish indistinct spots on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to velvety brown mold growth on the corresponding lower leaf surface
Leaves curling, withering, and dropping prematurely from bottom to top of plant
Blossom blighting and rare fruit calyx rot
causes: Fungal pathogen Passalora fulva
Relative humidity exceeding 85% with temperatures between 21-24°C
Dense, unpruned canopies and lack of ventilation in high tunnels or greenhouses
treatment: Apply copper fungicides or bio-fungicides at early disease onset
Prune lower foliage and sucker shoots to open up the canopy
Reduce greenhouse relative humidity through exhaust fans, heating, and ventilation
prevention: Maintain relative humidity below 85% in protected greenhouse environments
Plant leaf mold-resistant tomato hybrids (carrying Cf resistance genes)
Space plants generously and prune suckers to encourage continuous airflow
Avoid overhead misting and keep leaves dry

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. It is characterized by hundreds of tiny circular spots with grey centers and dark margins on lower leaves.
symptoms: Numerous small (1/16 to 1/8 inch), circular spots on lower leaves
Spots having dark brown borders with light grey or tan centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) visible inside the grey centers
Leaves turning yellow, withering, and dropping prematurely
causes: Fungal pathogen Septoria lycopersici
Overwintering in tomato crop residue and solanaceous weeds (such as nightshade)
Rain splashing and wet foliage over extended periods
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or Copper Hydroxide) at first symptom appearance
Apply bio-fungicides (Bacillus subtilis) for organic gardening
Prune and discard infected lower leaves promptly
prevention: Apply mulch around the base of plants to create a physical barrier against soil splashing
Prune lower foliage to keep leaves at least 12 inches above the soil surface
Water at root level via drip irrigation; avoid sprinkler watering
Practice 3-year crop rotation and eradicate wild nightshade weeds

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) are minute arachnid pests that pierce leaf cells to suck sap, causing yellow stippling, bronze foliage, and delicate webbing.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling dots on upper leaf surfaces
Leaves turning bronze, pale, dry, and brittle
Fine silk webbing visible on the undersides of leaves and growing shoot tips
Stunted plant growth and premature leaf drop in hot, dry weather
causes: Arthropod pest Tetranychus urticae
Hot, dry, and dusty weather conditions favoring rapid mite reproduction
Overuse of broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural mite predators
treatment: Spray undersides of leaves with Insecticidal Soap, Neem Oil, or Horticultural Oil
Apply selective miticides (such as Abamectin or Bifenazate) for severe commercial infestations
Release biological predatory mites (such as Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus)
Spray foliage with high-pressure water jets to knock down mite colonies and webbing
prevention: Keep garden pathways watered or mulched to minimize dust that repels beneficial predators
Ensure tomato plants are well-watered and not subjected to drought stress
Avoid preventative broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroid sprays that eliminate predator insects

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Tomato target spot is caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola. It creates brown lesions with pale centers and dark concentric rings on leaves, stems, and fruit.
symptoms: Small brown pinpoint spots on leaves expanding into circular lesions with light brown centers
Concentric rings visible in older lesions resembling target boards
Extensive leaf yellowing and premature defoliation
Sunken circular lesions with dark centers on tomato fruit
causes: Fungal pathogen Corynespora cassiicola
Warm temperatures (20-28°C) combined with high relative humidity and leaf wetness
Overwintering in old infected plant debris
treatment: Apply protective and systemic fungicides (such as Azoxystrobin, Chlorothalonil, or Boscalid)
Use copper-based fungicides for organic disease management
Prune infected foliage and improve canopy airflow
prevention: Provide wide plant spacing and prune suckers to promote air circulation
Mulch soil around plants to prevent soil-to-leaf splashing
Avoid overhead watering and irrigate only in early morning
Rotate out of solanaceous crops for 2-3 years

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: TYLCV is a devastating geminivirus transmitted by the sweetpotato/silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). It causes severe stunting, upward leaf curling, and total crop failure.
symptoms: Severe upward cupping and curling of leaf margins
Interveinal chlorosis and yellowing on young leaves
Extreme plant stunting with a bushy, erect 'bonsai' appearance
Flowers dropping prematurely, with virtually no fruit setting if infected early
causes: Virus (Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Begomovirus)
Insect transmission by the whitefly vector Bemisia tabaci
Movement of infected transplant seedlings across regions
treatment: There is no chemical cure for plant viral infections
Rogue out and destroy infected plants immediately inside sealed bags to prevent whitefly dispersal
Control whitefly insect populations using insecticidal soaps, neem oil, or systemic insecticides (such as Dinotefuran)
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato hybrids (carrying Ty-1, Ty-2, or Ty-3 resistance genes)
Install fine insect mesh netting (50-mesh) on greenhouse vents to block whiteflies
Place yellow sticky cards around crops to detect and trap early whitefly migrants
Reflective silver mulches to disorient whiteflies and deter landing

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV) is a highly stable, mechanically transmitted tobamovirus. It causes mottled light and dark green patterns on leaves, fern-like leaf distortion, and internal fruit browning.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on foliage
Distorted, blistered, or narrow 'fern-like' (stringy) leaves ('shoestringing')
Stunted plant growth and reduced vigor
Internal brown browning (vascular necrosis) inside fruit flesh
causes: Tobamovirus (Tomato Mosaic Virus)
Extremely stable virus transmitted by mechanical contact (hands, tools, grafting)
Infected seed or contaminated tobacco products handled by workers
treatment: There is no cure for virally infected plants
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Disinfect all tools, stakes, and greenhouse surfaces with 20% non-fat dry milk or 10% TSP (Trisodium Phosphate)
prevention: Plant certified virus-free seeds and resistant tomato varieties (marked 'T' or 'ToMV')
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water before handling tomato plants (especially if using tobacco)
Disinfect pruning shears regularly between each plant
Avoid planting tomatoes in soil containing un-decomposed infected roots

Tomato___healthy.description: The tomato plant exhibits lush deep green foliage, sturdy stems, and clean blossoms with no symptoms of fungal blights, bacterial spots, or viruses.
symptoms: Deep green, crisp foliage with healthy leaflet margins
Sturdy main stems with strong blossom clusters and fruit set
Clean leaf surfaces free of lesions, mold, or insect webs
causes: Optimal sun, fertile well-drained soil, balanced calcium and N-P-K nutrition, and root-level watering
treatment: No disease treatment required
Maintain consistent deep watering and organic mulch layer
prevention: Prune lower suckers and bottom leaves to maintain 12 inches of clearance above ground
Maintain mulch barrier over soil to prevent future pathogen splash
Inspect leaf undersides weekly for early signs of pests or spotting
